title: Multi-hop retrieval: build evidence chains with bounded searches
summary: Answer questions whose facts sit in separate documents without letting a plausible first hit become an unsupported final answer.
body:
Answer questions whose facts sit in separate documents without letting a plausible first hit become an unsupported final answer.

Represent the missing link

A multi-hop question needs two or more supported joins. A support ticket may name shipment SH-47, while the carrier notice names only its dispatch batch. First retrieve the ticket and extract its batch ID. Then search that exact ID in the permitted carrier corpus. Keep each edge as a tuple of source passage, extracted entity, target passage and match rule. The final answer must cite both ends of the join. Claim support should reject a chain whose second edge is only a semantic resemblance.

Search in a fixed budget

Give each hop its own candidate limit, time limit and permission filter. The planner can propose the next lookup, but application code should validate the proposed identifier against the preceding passage before executing it. Stop after a bounded number of hops; a loop between two documents is a failed search, not deeper reasoning. If the first document names two batches, branch into two explicit chains and keep their evidence separate until a source disambiguates them.

Preserve uncertainty

The chain may support that SH-47 belongs to batch BX-83 and that BX-83 was delayed. It does not prove the customer's delivery date changed unless a permitted source states that consequence. Distinguish a missing edge from a contradictory edge. Missing means the lookup exhausted its budget; contradictory means two eligible sources disagree and require revision or time resolution. Abstention is the correct output when a required edge has no evidence.

Evaluate the joins

Judgments should name the expected intermediate entity and answer-bearing passages, not only the answer text. Record success at hop one, success at hop two, chain precision and final claim support independently. A fluent answer can hide a bad join. Include decoy IDs with similar spelling, revoked passages, duplicate entity names across tenants and an answer that requires three documents. A single overall accuracy score will obscure which hop fails.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Evidence:
    passage_id: str
    tenant: str
    entity_id: str
    linked_id: str

def trace_shipment(shipment_id: str, tenant: str,
                   tickets: list[Evidence], notices: list[Evidence]) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    chains = []
    for ticket in tickets:
        if ticket.tenant != tenant or ticket.entity_id != shipment_id:
            continue
        for notice in notices:
            if notice.tenant == tenant and notice.entity_id == ticket.linked_id:
                chains.append((ticket.passage_id, notice.passage_id))
    return chains

tickets = [Evidence("ticket-47-r2", "north", "SH-47", "BX-83")]
notices = [Evidence("notice-83-r4", "north", "BX-83", "late"),
           Evidence("notice-83-private", "south", "BX-83", "cancelled")]
assert trace_shipment("SH-47", "north", tickets, notices) == [
    ("ticket-47-r2", "notice-83-r4")]
assert trace_shipment("SH-47", "south", tickets, notices) == []

Performance and operating cost

The transparent nested-loop baseline costs O(TN) time for T tickets and N notices and O(C) space for C chains. Index notices by tenant and entity to reduce the join to O(T + N + C) build-and-probe time. Each extra retrieval hop adds latency and new failure opportunities, so cap depth and branch count before generation.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a model-generated intermediate ID that is absent from the cited passage.
  • Combining passages from different tenants because the entity text matches.
  • Claiming a downstream consequence that neither source states.
  • Allowing repeated hops to search indefinitely.

Validation drill

Create 37 questions: 19 valid two-hop chains, six ambiguous branches, five missing second edges, four decoy IDs and three revoked intermediates. Report first-hop and full-chain recall separately.

title: Table retrieval: keep numeric cells attached to their labels
summary: Retrieve tabular evidence without losing row keys, column units, revision dates or the calculation needed for an answer.
body:
Retrieve tabular evidence without losing row keys, column units, revision dates or the calculation needed for an answer.

Treat a cell as a qualified fact

The value 47 has no useful meaning alone. A searchable fact needs table ID, revision, row key, column name, unit, effective period and access label. Store a compact row rendering for discovery, but preserve typed cells for comparison and arithmetic. A question about the West queue's 47-hour target must not match a North queue row or a 47-day retention policy. Extraction provenance should point back to the original table location.

Separate discovery from computation

Use lexical or semantic search to locate a candidate table, then execute an approved operation over its typed rows. Do not derive a total by reading the top few text snippets; omitted rows silently bias the result. Exact row and column filters should run before aggregation. If the requested metric is not defined, ask for the metric rather than inventing a sum. Record the row IDs used so the answer can be audited after a table revision.

Handle headers and units

Merged headings, repeated page headers and blank cells need explicit parsing rules. A blank value can mean unknown, not zero. A percentage column cannot be summed like a count, and a currency column cannot be combined across currencies without a declared conversion rule. If a table changes from hours to minutes in a new revision, the retrieval layer must not silently mix both. Index swaps should move the searchable row text and typed table together.

Test answer coverage

Judged queries should include an exact cell lookup, a filter plus sum, a percentage with denominator, a missing cell and a superseded revision. Evaluate table discovery separately from calculation correctness. A system that retrieves the right table but adds the wrong rows still fails. For each calculated answer, retain the operation, selected row keys, table revision and resulting value.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class QueueRow:
    region: str
    week: int
    resolved: int | None
    revision: str

def resolved_total(rows: list[QueueRow], region: str, weeks: set[int],
                   revision: str) -> int:
    selected = [row for row in rows if row.region == region
                and row.week in weeks and row.revision == revision]
    if len(selected) != len(weeks) or any(row.resolved is None for row in selected):
        raise ValueError("incomplete table coverage")
    if len({row.week for row in selected}) != len(selected):
        raise ValueError("duplicate row key")
    return sum(row.resolved for row in selected if row.resolved is not None)

queue_rows = [QueueRow("West", 31, 47, "r8"),
              QueueRow("West", 32, 29, "r8"),
              QueueRow("North", 31, 81, "r8")]
assert resolved_total(queue_rows, "West", {31, 32}, "r8") == 76
try:
    resolved_total(queue_rows, "West", {31, 33}, "r8")
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("missing week was accepted")

Performance and operating cost

The baseline scans N rows in O(N) time and stores O(K) selected rows. A typed index on revision, region and week avoids a full scan in a large warehouse; query cost then depends on matching rows and index lookup. Preserve row lineage even if it adds metadata, because a wrong numeric answer is harder to diagnose than a slow lookup.

Common Mistakes

  • Embedding isolated numeric cells without their row and column labels.
  • Treating blank cells as zero during aggregation.
  • Summing a top-k snippet sample instead of the full filtered table.
  • Combining rows from different revisions or units.

Validation drill

Build a 29-row queue table with two revisions and three regions. Answer 12 cell questions and eight aggregate questions. Make two cells blank and one row duplicated; require explicit errors for both cases.

title: Multimodal retrieval: connect images, OCR and text to one asset identity
summary: Search image-bearing documents while keeping captions, OCR text, crop coordinates and permissions tied to the exact source revision.
body:
Search image-bearing documents while keeping captions, OCR text, crop coordinates and permissions tied to the exact source revision.

Define the asset graph

A diagram may have a text caption, OCR labels, a surrounding paragraph and a visual embedding. Give all views one immutable asset revision, then store their own modality and location. A match in OCR is evidence for visible words, not for a visual relation that OCR cannot read. A visual similarity match locates candidate images; it does not prove that two valves have the same operating limit. Source provenance must survive the modality change.

Retrieve and fuse carefully

Text queries can search captions and OCR; image queries can use visual embeddings. Fuse candidate asset IDs only after permission and revision checks. Preserve the match route in the result: caption, OCR, surrounding text or image similarity. This matters when a reviewer asks why a drawing ranked first. Rerank with the full question and a bounded set of candidate assets, not a collection of detached crop embeddings.

Resolve the cited region

An answer about a label in the upper-left crop should cite that region and its parent page. Store normalized crop coordinates and the original image dimensions so a viewer can highlight the right area. If preprocessing rotates or resizes the image, transform coordinates back before presenting them. A citation to an entire manual page may be too broad when the claim depends on a tiny annotation. Support checks should confirm the cited modality can prove the claim.

Measure modality-specific misses

Maintain query slices for exact OCR strings, paraphrased captions, visual resemblance and questions requiring both text and image. Evaluate candidate recall by modality and asset revision. A high combined score can conceal that OCR systematically misses rotated labels. Keep a no-answer slice where a visually similar image lacks the requested label, and require the system to say so.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AssetView:
    asset_id: str
    revision: str
    tenant: str
    modality: str
    content: str

def find_label(views: list[AssetView], label: str, tenant: str,
               active_revisions: dict[str, str]) -> list[str]:
    return sorted({view.asset_id for view in views
                   if view.tenant == tenant and view.modality == "ocr"
                   and active_revisions.get(view.asset_id) == view.revision
                   and label.casefold() in view.content.casefold()})

views = [AssetView("pump-47", "r3", "plant-a", "ocr", "Outlet 47 kPa"),
         AssetView("pump-47", "r2", "plant-a", "ocr", "Outlet 73 kPa"),
         AssetView("pump-47", "r3", "plant-b", "ocr", "Outlet 47 kPa")]
assert find_label(views, "47 kPa", "plant-a", {"pump-47": "r3"}) == ["pump-47"]
assert find_label(views, "73 kPa", "plant-a", {"pump-47": "r3"}) == []

Performance and operating cost

The sample scans V views in O(V) time and uses O(A) result space for A matching assets. Production retrieval can index each modality, but storage and embedding work grow with the number of views and crops. Set crop limits and deduplicate near-identical renders; otherwise one document can flood the candidate window.

Common Mistakes

  • Using visual similarity as proof of a printed numeric label.
  • Returning a crop without its parent asset and revision.
  • Mixing a fresh caption with OCR from an old image revision.
  • Showing a broad page citation when only one crop supports the answer.

Validation drill

Index 17 diagrams with captions and OCR, including three rotated scans and two superseded revisions. Judge exact-label, visual and mixed queries separately; verify every cited crop opens at the correct page and coordinates.

title: Incremental retrieval ingestion: replay events without reviving deleted passages
summary: Apply document revisions, permission changes and deletions safely when source events arrive late, twice or out of order.
body:
Apply document revisions, permission changes and deletions safely when source events arrive late, twice or out of order.

Make the event contract explicit

Each source event needs tenant, document ID, monotonic source version, action and a stable event ID. The index writer should compare versions before replacing passages. At-least-once delivery means duplicate events are normal; processing the same revision twice must yield the same searchable state. A late upsert for version 6 cannot restore a document deleted at version 8. Index freshness depends on this ordering rule.

Separate removal from embedding work

Delete and permission-revocation events should invalidate answer caches and remove eligible passages promptly. A new revision may take longer because extraction and embeddings run asynchronously. During that interval, either keep an explicitly permitted old revision under a defined policy or mark the document unavailable. Do not show a half-written revision whose metadata and vectors disagree. Publish the new generation only after all required passages and filters are ready.

Retain a tombstone

A tombstone records the latest delete version even after the vector rows are removed. Without it, a replayed old upsert can recreate a deleted passage. Keep the tombstone until upstream retention guarantees make older events impossible, and test that guarantee rather than guessing. A permission change also needs a versioned marker; it may be independent of content revision and should not wait for re-embedding.

Observe lag and recovery

Measure event age at application, pending extraction count, index generation and deletion-to-unavailability delay. Replay a durable event log into a staging index, compare eligible document sets, then atomically switch the alias. Encoder migrations need the same generation boundary. A process restart should resume from a checkpoint without losing the version guard.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DocumentEvent:
    document_id: str
    version: int
    action: str
    text: str = ""

def apply_event(state: dict[str, tuple[int, str | None]],
                event: DocumentEvent) -> None:
    current_version = state.get(event.document_id, (-1, None))[0]
    if event.version <= current_version:
        return
    if event.action == "delete":
        state[event.document_id] = (event.version, None)
    elif event.action == "upsert" and event.text.strip():
        state[event.document_id] = (event.version, event.text)
    else:
        raise ValueError("invalid document event")

index_state: dict[str, tuple[int, str | None]] = {}
apply_event(index_state, DocumentEvent("policy-47", 8, "delete"))
apply_event(index_state, DocumentEvent("policy-47", 6, "upsert", "old policy"))
apply_event(index_state, DocumentEvent("policy-47", 8, "delete"))
assert index_state["policy-47"] == (8, None)

Performance and operating cost

The version guard is O(1) expected time per event with a hash map and O(D) state for D documents. Extraction and embedding dominate CPU and queue time. Tombstones consume storage, but deleting them too early risks data resurrection. Report end-to-end publication lag and revocation lag separately.

Common Mistakes

  • Deleting vector rows without retaining the latest source version.
  • Assuming queue delivery is exactly once or ordered across partitions.
  • Waiting for slow re-embedding before enforcing a permission revocation.
  • Publishing metadata for a new revision before its passage set is complete.

Validation drill

Replay 53 events with duplicates, delayed upserts, revisions and deletes into an empty index. Shuffle events while preserving per-document source versions; assert that eligible final documents and tombstones match the source of truth.

  • Embedding migrations: keep query and document vectors in one space
  • Retrieval caches and conversation turns: recheck access every time

title: Retrieval traces: locate the stage that lost the answer
summary: Trace routing, filtering, candidate generation, reranking and context packing so a failed answer can be explained and repaired.
body:
Trace routing, filtering, candidate generation, reranking and context packing so a failed answer can be explained and repaired.

Record stage boundaries

A single total latency and final answer are not enough. Give each query a trace ID and record route, index generation, encoder revision, allowed corpus scope, candidate counts, reranker cutoff, context IDs and answer citations. Keep the original query in a protected audit store when policy permits; avoid putting private text, user IDs or document contents into metric labels. Routing and packing need separate spans.

Name the first failing stage

If the answer-bearing passage is absent from candidate retrieval, changing the prompt will not fix it. If it appears at rank 12 but the reranker receives only eight, the candidate window is the failure. If it reaches the context packet but the model cites another passage, investigate answer synthesis and support checking. Diagnose against a judged passage ID, not a vague statement that search felt poor.

Keep traces safe and bounded

Trace metadata can itself expose sensitive document names or tenant relationships. Hash or redact identifiers in broad telemetry, reserve full IDs for access-controlled debugging, and apply retention limits. Sample routine traffic, but retain all permission denials, deletion races and release-gate failures under an approved policy. A trace with every passage text can cost more to store than the retrieved context and may violate the source's access boundary.

Use paired comparisons

Replay a fixed query against current and candidate releases with the same corpus snapshot and permission scope. Diff each stage: route, top-k identities, filters, rerank order, context selection and citations. This isolates a changed encoder from a changed index or prompt. Release gates should attach these traces to failures so a rollback decision has evidence.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RetrievalTrace:
    expected_passage: str
    candidates: tuple[str, ...]
    reranked: tuple[str, ...]
    context: tuple[str, ...]
    cited: tuple[str, ...]

def first_loss(trace: RetrievalTrace) -> str:
    stages = (("candidate retrieval", trace.candidates),
              ("reranking", trace.reranked),
              ("context packing", trace.context),
              ("answer citation", trace.cited))
    for stage_name, passage_ids in stages:
        if trace.expected_passage not in passage_ids:
            return stage_name
    return "supported path"

incident = RetrievalTrace("policy-47-r3", ("policy-47-r3", "memo-29"),
                          ("memo-29",), ("memo-29",), ("memo-29",))
assert first_loss(incident) == "reranking"
assert first_loss(RetrievalTrace("missing", (), (), (), ())) == "candidate retrieval"

Performance and operating cost

Finding the first loss scans at most the four recorded stage lists, O(K) time for K total IDs and O(1) extra space. A full trace pipeline adds serialization, storage and review cost proportional to captured candidates. Sample successful queries and store compact IDs; preserve richer traces for judged failures under access control.

Common Mistakes

  • Blaming generation when the answer passage never entered candidate retrieval.
  • Logging private passage text or principal IDs in broad metric labels.
  • Comparing releases against different corpus snapshots.
  • Recording only final scores and losing stage identities.

Validation drill

Create 41 judged traces with deliberate failures at each stage. Produce a count by first-loss stage and inspect one trace from each category before changing any retrieval parameter.

title: Query expansion: add recall terms without changing the user's question
summary: Use controlled synonyms and subqueries while retaining exact IDs, exclusions, dates and authorization scope.
body:
Use controlled synonyms and subqueries while retaining exact IDs, exclusions, dates and authorization scope.

Split immutable constraints from optional terms

Parse exact identifiers, quoted phrases, exclusions, tenant scope and time bounds before expansion. Keep those constraints attached to every generated subquery. A query for case AX-47 after September must not turn into a general query about delayed cases. Expansion is useful for vocabulary mismatch: ‘chargeback’ may appear as ‘payment dispute’ in a permitted document. It is not permission to relax an exact case ID. Routing should decide whether expansion is needed at all.

Bound candidates and weights

Start with a small, reviewed synonym list or a validated reformulator. Search the original query as one leg and each expansion as a separate leg, then merge by passage ID. Preserve which leg found each candidate. Weight the original query and exact-match leg so a broad synonym cannot bury the literal target. Rank fusion is a useful merge baseline because score scales from different legs are not directly comparable.

Reject drift

A proposed rewrite fails when it drops an identifier, changes a number, reverses a negation, broadens a tenant, or shifts a date interval. Compare parsed constraints before executing the rewrite. Some vocabulary changes are context dependent: ‘hold’ can mean a payment hold or warehouse hold. For ambiguous terms, retrieve with both senses only inside the authorized corpus and let evidence disambiguate; otherwise ask the user.

Measure value by query family

Expansion should improve recall for jargon and paraphrase queries without harming exact-ID precision or latency. Build paired judgments with original-only and expanded runs. Report newly found answer passages, false positives, average additional calls and p95 latency. Retain a no-answer set; a system that answers more questions by matching unrelated synonyms has not improved. Traces should expose which expansion introduced each candidate.

Worked contract

import re

def safe_expansions(question: str, synonyms: dict[str, tuple[str, ...]]) -> list[str]:
    required_ids = set(re.findall(r"\bAX-\d+\b", question.upper()))
    variants = [question]
    for term, replacements in synonyms.items():
        if not re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(term)}\b", question, re.IGNORECASE):
            continue
        for replacement in replacements[:2]:
            candidate = re.sub(rf"\b{re.escape(term)}\b", replacement,
                               question, count=1, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
            if required_ids <= set(re.findall(r"\bAX-\d+\b", candidate.upper())):
                variants.append(candidate)
    return variants[:4]

variants = safe_expansions("AX-47 chargeback status",
                           {"chargeback": ("payment dispute", "card dispute")})
assert variants == ["AX-47 chargeback status",
                    "AX-47 payment dispute status", "AX-47 card dispute status"]
assert all("AX-47" in variant for variant in variants)

Performance and operating cost

For Q query characters and at most S reviewed replacements, this small implementation scans O(SQ) time and stores at most four variants. Search cost can grow roughly with the number of variants, so cap expansion count and parallel calls. This demonstration protects exact IDs only; production validation must also compare negations, dates, tenant scope and other parsed constraints before dispatch.

Common Mistakes

  • Replacing an exact identifier with a likely-looking related identifier.
  • Dropping ‘not’ or a date bound while rewriting.
  • Merging scores from different search legs as if their scales were equal.
  • Celebrating recall gains without measuring no-answer false positives.

Validation drill

Judge 61 requests across exact IDs, jargon synonyms, negations, date bounds and no-answer cases. Compare original-only search with a maximum of three expanded variants; reject any rewrite that changes parsed constraints.

title: Retrieval-based AI
summary: Ground generated answers in permitted, current documents and measure retrieval separately from response quality.
body:
Ground generated answers in permitted, current documents and measure retrieval separately from response quality.

Where to begin

Start with the corpus contract: document identity, ownership, revision, and deletion. Then work through chunk boundaries, lexical and dense retrieval, reranking, evidence support, abstention, prompt injection, and evaluation. The project tests no-answer and restricted-document cases, not just successful lookups.

Choose the right method

More retrieved chunks consume context, latency, and token budget. Improve candidate recall and evidence ranking before increasing the window; a long prompt cannot recover a relevant passage that the index never returned.

Do not let retrieved text issue instructions to a tool or override access rules. A fluent answer without a supporting passage should fail the evidence check.

title: Claim-level citations: verify each answer against its passage
summary: Bind each factual claim to a permitted, current passage and reject citations that are merely related to the topic.
body:
Bind each factual claim to a permitted, current passage and reject citations that are merely related to the topic.

Split answers into testable claims

‘Refunds arrive in 47 hours and managers can extend the window’ contains two claims. Each needs support from the selected evidence packet. A policy-title citation is too broad when its quoted span states only the first clause. Keep claim and passage IDs together. Distinguish direct support, contradiction, insufficient evidence and facts supplied by the user. Abstention is correct when a required claim lacks support.

Check passage identity

The cited span must belong to an active permitted revision and have been included in the generator context. Resolve it to a readable page or section. A valid-looking ID for a retired revision is insufficient. Extraction provenance supplies the source location.

Test support rather than overlap

A passage about refund windows may omit the 47-hour value. ‘Up to 47 hours’ does not justify ‘always within 47 hours.’ Numbers, negation, dates and exceptions deserve explicit checks. An entailment model can triage cases, but its confidence alone does not prove support; keep a human-judged sample.

Fail clearly

Remove or qualify unsupported claims and regenerate from the same permitted packet. If the core question remains unanswered, state which part cannot be verified. Log the unsupported claim and citation ID without putting private source text in public telemetry. Count unsupported-claim rate separately from retrieval misses.

Worked contract

def validate_claim_citations(claims: list[dict], packet_ids: set[str],
                             active_ids: set[str]) -> list[str]:
    failures = []
    for claim in claims:
        cited = set(claim["citations"])
        if not cited or not cited <= packet_ids or not cited <= active_ids:
            failures.append(claim["claim_id"])
        elif claim["support"] != "supported":
            failures.append(claim["claim_id"])
    return failures

claims = [{"claim_id": "hours", "citations": ["policy-r8-p4"], "support": "supported"},
          {"claim_id": "extension", "citations": ["policy-r8-p4"], "support": "insufficient"}]
assert validate_claim_citations(claims, {"policy-r8-p4"}, {"policy-r8-p4"}) == ["extension"]

Performance and operating cost

Identity checking takes O(C + E) expected time for C claims and E citation edges, with O(C) failure output. Semantic support review is costlier and may need model calls or human adjudication. Sample high-impact claims first; do not hide unsupported claims in an average answer score.

Common Mistakes

  • Accepting a citation because its document title matches the topic.
  • Using a retired passage or one absent from the final context packet.
  • Treating ‘up to’ and ‘always’ as equivalent.
  • Reporting retrieval recall as proof of answer support.

Validation drill

Write 29 answers with a numeric claim, an exception and a distractor citation each. Mark support from the exact packet and count unsupported claims that survive automation.

title: Document extraction: preserve passage provenance through OCR and parsing
summary: Turn source files into searchable passages while retaining the page, section, revision and extraction quality needed to verify an answer.
body:
Turn source files into searchable passages while retaining the page, section, revision and extraction quality needed to verify an answer.

Define the extracted record

A text string alone is not a source. Each passage needs document ID, immutable revision ID, page or section, span offsets when available, extraction method, language and access label. A PDF policy may contain a scanned page, two-column layout and a table whose cells change meaning when read in the wrong order. Store the source file hash and parser version so a changed extraction can be rebuilt without pretending the document itself changed. Corpus identity is the parent contract.

Separate clean text from uncertain text

Parse machine-readable text first. Route image-only pages to OCR, and mark uncertain spans rather than silently normalizing them into authoritative policy. A table value of 47 under ‘hours’ is different from 47 under ‘days’; flattening the headers can invert a support rule. Keep table headers with row text or represent the table as structured cells. Human review should focus on low-confidence pages that answer high-impact questions, not every document equally.

Retain location through cleanup

Whitespace normalization, header removal and dehyphenation can improve search. They also shift character offsets. Maintain a map from cleaned spans back to source-page coordinates or stable section IDs. When the answer cites a passage, the reader should land on the source location that actually supports the claim. If an OCR run changes, rebuild the chunk IDs and invalidate answers tied to old offsets. Citation integrity depends on this map.

Gate ingestion with concrete failures

Feed the parser a missing page, duplicate footer, rotated scan, repeated table header and an inaccessible file. Reject a document if its required metadata or access label is absent. Record page count, extracted character count, empty pages and confidence distribution. A parser yielding text is not evidence that it preserved meaning. Compare a reviewed sample of passages against the original page, especially around headings, tables and footnotes.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
from hashlib import sha256

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExtractedPassage:
    document_id: str
    revision_id: str
    page: int
    section: str
    text: str
    source_sha256: str

def passage_record(document_id: str, revision_id: str, page: int,
                   section: str, text: str, source_bytes: bytes) -> ExtractedPassage:
    if page < 1 or not document_id or not revision_id or not section or not text.strip():
        raise ValueError("incomplete extraction provenance")
    return ExtractedPassage(document_id, revision_id, page, section,
                            text.strip(), sha256(source_bytes).hexdigest())

source = b"Policy r8 page 4"
passage = passage_record("refund-policy", "r8", 4, "Exceptions", " 47 hours ", source)
assert passage.page == 4 and passage.text == "47 hours"
assert passage.source_sha256 == sha256(source).hexdigest()

Performance and operating cost

Extraction is O(B) in source bytes before OCR; OCR cost also depends on page count and resolution. Provenance adds small metadata per passage, while page images and offset maps add storage. Budget retries by document, not an unbounded queue. Measure empty-page rate and reviewed semantic errors separately from parser throughput.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating OCR output as exact text without a confidence or review path.
  • Dropping table headers or section titles before chunking.
  • Reusing offsets after normalization changes the text.
  • Indexing a passage when its access label or revision is missing.

Validation drill

Extract a 23-page policy with a two-column page, one rotated scan and a table. Check five answer-bearing passages against their original page and record which parser change would invalidate each citation.

title: Index freshness: publish complete revisions and remove stale chunks
summary: Index updates need a versioned build, deletion handling and an atomic reader switch so answers never mix policy generations.
body:
Index updates need a versioned build, deletion handling and an atomic reader switch so answers never mix policy generations.

Build a candidate generation

When the support handbook changes, parse and index the new revision under a candidate generation. Keep the current generation serving while the candidate is incomplete. Validate document counts, active revisions, permissions and representative retrieval questions, then switch the reader pointer. Backfill publication] uses the same complete-before-visible idea.

Propagate deletion

A revoked policy can remain in an embedding index, lexical index or answer cache. Track document-to-chunk lineage so removal reaches every derived store. If a deletion cannot be completed promptly, deny access to the document ID at query time while reindexing catches up. Do not rely on an old vector disappearing merely because its source file was removed.

Choose freshness guarantees

Record ingestion lag, last successful index generation and maximum acceptable age. An urgent policy correction may require a synchronous block on old content; a routine edit may tolerate a short lag. Communicate when the answer feature is stale or unavailable rather than silently serving a superseded rule. No-answer behavior] can be safer during a gap.

Drill a partial failure

Fail one document during candidate indexing. The current generation should remain visible, the candidate should not publish, and an operator should see the rejected document and reason. Then revoke a permission and confirm query-time filtering blocks the old chunk before the next full rebuild.

Implementation

def publish_index(candidate, current_pointer, required_documents):
    if (set(candidate["document_ids"]) != set(required_documents)
            or len(candidate["document_ids"]) != len(set(candidate["document_ids"]))):
        raise ValueError("index generation is incomplete")
    if candidate["failed_chunks"] or not candidate["permission_checks_passed"]:
        raise ValueError("index generation failed checks")
    previous_generation = current_pointer.read()
    if not current_pointer.compare_and_swap(previous_generation, candidate["generation_id"]):
        raise RuntimeError("index pointer changed during publish")
    return previous_generation

Performance and operating cost

A full rebuild reads O(C) corpus content and creates O(K) chunks, embeddings and index entries. A pointer switch is cheap; storing two generations temporarily increases storage and build cost.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expose a partial candidate index.
  • Do not forget answer caches when deleting content.
  • Do not wait for full reindexing to revoke access.

title: Retrieval release gates: evaluate slices before changing an index
summary: Promote a retriever only after judged recall, support, access and latency checks pass for distinct query families.
body:
Promote a retriever only after judged recall, support, access and latency checks pass for distinct query families.

Freeze the comparison

Store query, permitted corpus snapshot, expected answer-bearing passage IDs, acceptable abstention and query family. Run current and candidate versions against the same access snapshot. Keep exact IDs, paraphrases, multilingual queries, long documents, stale revisions and no-answer cases separate. A global average can rise while one small tenant loses its only correct passage. Retrieval and answer quality remain separate measurements.

Measure decisions

For each query, measure answer-bearing candidate recall, required-fact survival in the final packet, first relevant rank and unsupported answer claims. Record p95 latency and forbidden-passage exposure; the latter must stay at zero. Some questions have no answer, so abstention matters. Compare equal cutoffs and token budgets across versions.

Set slice floors before testing

Write thresholds before seeing candidate results. A release may require no access violations, no decline in exact-ID recall and a bounded p95 increase while accepting a defined paraphrase improvement. Such thresholds are product policies, not universal constants. Inspect every newly failed query and retain it for regression work.

Canary and recover

After offline gates pass, send a small permitted traffic slice to the candidate alias and watch latency, empty-result rate and citation resolution before widening. Record encoder, extraction, corpus, filter and ranker revisions. Rollback query encoder and index alias together. Embedding migrations fail quietly when only one half is reverted.

Worked contract

def release_decision(current: dict, candidate: dict) -> tuple[bool, list[str]]:
    failures = []
    if candidate["access_violations"] != 0:
        failures.append("access violation")
    if candidate["exact_id_recall"] < current["exact_id_recall"]:
        failures.append("exact-ID recall regression")
    if candidate["answer_support"] < current["answer_support"]:
        failures.append("answer support regression")
    if candidate["p95_ms"] > current["p95_ms"] + 47:
        failures.append("latency budget exceeded")
    return not failures, failures

baseline = {"access_violations": 0, "exact_id_recall": .94,
            "answer_support": .91, "p95_ms": 168}
candidate = {"access_violations": 0, "exact_id_recall": .95,
             "answer_support": .92, "p95_ms": 199}
assert release_decision(baseline, candidate) == (True, [])
assert release_decision(baseline, {**candidate, "access_violations": 1})[0] is False

Performance and operating cost

Evaluation of Q queries and K candidates costs at least O(QK) identity work, plus search, rerank and answer calls. Keep a small smoke set for each change and a broader judged set before promotion. The 47 ms allowance in this example is product-specific; choose a measured budget for the actual service.

Common Mistakes

  • Promoting on one average while an important tenant slice regresses.
  • Changing the judged corpus between baseline and candidate runs.
  • Reporting answer quality without candidate recall or access exposure.
  • Rolling back the index while leaving the new query encoder active.

Validation drill

Build 120 judged questions across six slices. Compare two generations at identical top-12 and 600-token packet limits, list newly failed queries and record the rollback target.

title: Retrieval query routing: preserve exact constraints before search
summary: Route identifiers, policy questions and aggregate requests to the right evidence path without rewriting away the user's constraints.
body:
Route identifiers, policy questions and aggregate requests to the right evidence path without rewriting away the user's constraints.

Classify the request before reformulation

A question containing case ID AX-47 and an exact error string needs a literal lookup; a paraphrase of a policy may need semantic retrieval. A count of cases by week belongs to a governed query over structured data. Treat these as different jobs. Extract the requested output, exact tokens, tenant scope and time boundary first. A reformulator may add synonyms, but it cannot replace AX-47 with a more common case or turn a count into a prose summary. Candidate retrieval starts after this contract is fixed.

Keep routing observable

Record the selected path and the reason: exact ID, natural-language passage, structured aggregation, or mixed evidence. Run lexical and semantic search in parallel for mixed requests, then merge permitted candidates. A vector match can help find related language, but it cannot establish that a literal identifier was present. If a required identifier is absent from the result, reject that candidate even when its embedding score is high. A SQL query must use an approved metric definition; generated SQL is not a substitute for permission checks.

Handle ambiguous follow-ups

For ‘What changed after that?’, resolve ‘that’ from the current conversation only when a single permitted document identity is clear. Carry the resolved ID, revision and time window into the new query. If two incidents were discussed, ask which one the user means. Never copy a previous user's context or a past authorization decision into a new session. Conversation boundaries need the same rigor as document permissions.

Evaluate the router as a component

Create a labeled set with identifiers, paraphrases, mixed questions, unsupported aggregates and ambiguous follow-ups. Count wrong-route decisions separately from search misses. An exact-search route can fail because the identifier was parsed incorrectly; a semantic route can fail because its candidate pool omitted the answer. Store the original query beside the routed form so reviewers can see what changed. Include at least one question where no source is eligible and require the no-answer path.

Worked contract

def route_support_query(question: str, case_ids: set[str]) -> dict[str, object]:
    import re
    requested_ids = set(re.findall(r"\bAX-\d+\b", question.upper()))
    unknown_ids = requested_ids - case_ids
    if unknown_ids:
        return {"route": "no_match", "ids": sorted(unknown_ids)}
    if re.search(r"\b(count|how many|per week)\b", question.lower()):
        return {"route": "aggregate", "ids": sorted(requested_ids)}
    if requested_ids:
        return {"route": "hybrid_exact_first", "ids": sorted(requested_ids)}
    return {"route": "semantic", "ids": []}

known_cases = {"AX-47", "AX-63"}
assert route_support_query("Why did AX-47 retry?", known_cases)["route"] == "hybrid_exact_first"
assert route_support_query("Count AX-63 cases per week", known_cases)["route"] == "aggregate"
assert route_support_query("Explain AX-91", known_cases)["route"] == "no_match"

Performance and operating cost

Routing costs O(q + m) time for query length q and m extracted IDs in this small example. The expensive work is downstream: two search legs, an aggregation or a clarification turn. Log wrong-route rates by query family and cap simultaneous searches; a cheap router that silently drops an exact constraint wastes the entire answer pipeline.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating an embedding score as proof of an exact case-ID match.
  • Rewriting a user-specified date or identifier without retaining the original constraint.
  • Sending an aggregate question to passage search and inventing a count from snippets.
  • Resolving an ambiguous follow-up from a different session.

Validation drill

Build 47 labeled queries: 12 exact IDs, 12 paraphrases, 11 mixed requests, six aggregates and six ambiguous follow-ups. Report route accuracy for each family and inspect every false route before changing a threshold.
